otherProblems: G-6/G-7 (empty values): the preset box renders as a small empty outlined rectangle beside 'OPENING STATEMENTS' — a shape holding nothing; it should collapse when the field is blank.
G-24–G-29 (penalty): the red '-10' badge is placed directly on the centre divider line; the pill's fill hides the rule, but it reads as a badge parked on a line rather than in a space of its own.

G-4/G-5/G-8/G-9 (long values): the left speaker's name slot shows '180' while the clock reads 05:05, which suggests the field order/labels the stress harness inferred do not match what the graphic renders — worth checking the control-panel field labels so the operator is not confused.
G-14 (Take, 300 ms): rows are revealed by a slide-up mask so letters are cut mid-glyph for a few frames; it reads as a deliberate wipe, not a layout fault.
answer.reasons: A clean, well-proportioned two-sided clock: both sides get equal space, type is large and readable on both grounds, the active side is clearly marked by the full accent bar and orange clock, and long round labels, side labels and names wrap inside their columns without clipping or overlap. Switch, penalty and reset all do what the brief asks and the frames show the results (right clock takes over and counts; -10 deducted with a red flash; both clocks back to 05:00). The only visible blemishes are an empty outlined preset box when that field is blank and the -10 badge sitting on the divider — nits a director would accept rather than pull the graphic for.

otherProblems: After the Take no speaker is active (both clocks sit at 180 through 10 s), so the Penalty press in G-24–G-29 produces no visible change; penalty only has an effect once Switch has been used (its effect on a running clock is never shown).
Empty-values state (G-6/G-7) leaves an empty outlined badge box beside DEBATE and two orphan gold dashes with nothing under them.

In the one-sided stress frames (G-8–G-11) the side carrying a speaker name pushes its clock ~20 px lower than the other side, so the two clocks no longer sit on one baseline; the small grey '180' label above the long name reads as an orphan number.
Take/Out use a mask reveal, so mid-transition frames (G-15, G-43, G-44) briefly show text half-revealed; settled frames are clean.
answer.reasons: A tidy, balanced two-sided clock: dark centred panel with a gold baseline, title and 'SEC EACH' badge centred, equal columns for Proposition and Opposition with large readable clocks, and every value (including the long title, long names and six-digit clocks) stays inside its field with good contrast on both grounds. Switch visibly activates a side (gold text and extended accent line) and the clock counts down; Reset returns both to 180 and clears the active state; the operator surface offers switch, penalty and reset. The weaknesses are behavioural rather than visual: no speaker is active straight after the Take so penalty does nothing until a switch, and the empty-values state leaves an empty badge outline, but the on-air states a viewer would normally see are clean.

otherProblems: G-4/G-5/G-27: the long footer value is cut at a word boundary ('…VOTING IS') with no ellipsis, so it reads as an unfinished sentence; not mid-glyph and not spilling, but a silent truncation.
G-4/G-5: with long kicker and question the panel grows upward to about y=452, slightly above the midline the brief asks for.
G-6/G-7: with empty values the panel collapses to the kicker plus a bare rule over empty space; an edge state an operator would not normally take to air.
G-22: during Out the bars empty before the percentages fade, a brief transitional inconsistency a viewer would barely notice.
answer.reasons: A clean, well-structured vote board: kicker, question, four labelled rows with bars and right-aligned percentages, and a status footer, all left-anchored in the lower half with a single yellow accent bar. The leading option is clearly ahead (yellow bar, white bold label, yellow figure) against grey runners-up, and everything is readable on both the dark studio plate and the light ground. Long values wrap inside the panel and the panel grows to hold them; Take, Update and Out are tidy. The only blemishes are a word-boundary truncation of the stress footer and the panel creeping above the midline under long text, neither of which a director would pull it for.

basicMistakes.where: Long-value state: the question slot under AUDIENCE VOTE shows the raw pipe-delimited options string ('…read in full|A second long option that competes|Third'), and the single option row holds the question text wrapped over five lines beside an empty track with no percentage — no option names or percentages appear anywhere.
Same broken long-value render on the light ground: raw '|' separators in the question slot, question text in the option row, empty bar, no percentage.

After the Update to long options, the option row text ('Which of the three proposals should the student union bring to the board this semester?') wraps to four lines and its last two lines run below the bottom edge of the dark panel onto the video (also visible in G-14 to G-17).
Updated board collapses to one option row with a bar but no percentage figure and no other options; the vote content the brief needs is gone.

otherProblems: In the long-value frames the text pushed into the question slot is set small and bold (roughly 18 px) with visible '|' characters — too small for television and clearly a parsing failure on screen.
Take and Out transitions and the sample-value layout (G-2, G-3, G-6, G-7) are otherwise clean, well-spaced and readable, with the leader clearly highlighted.
answer.reasons: With the brief's sample values this is a tidy, readable vote panel: clear question, three rows, leader highlighted in amber, percentages aligned, and clean Take/Out animations. But it falls apart under the stress values: the long options are dumped as a raw pipe-separated string into the question slot while the question text lands in the option row with an empty bar and no percentage, and after the Update the wrapped text spills out below the panel edge with the percentages gone entirely. A director cannot put on a graphic that breaks the moment the operator enters realistic option text.
